name: Johor Sultanate
line: Speak gently, honour custom, repay kindness and work alongside your neighbours.

quote.text: Golden bananas carried on a voyage, one ripens on top of the chest. A debt of gold can be repaid; a debt of kindness is carried to the grave.
quote.source: Traditional. Pisang emas dibawa belayar, masak sebiji di atas peti; hutang emas boleh dibayar, hutang budi dibawa mati

quotes.text: If you wish to know a person of good breeding, look to their conduct and their speech.
quotes.source: Gurindam Dua Belas, the Twelve Gurindam, fifth section, written on Penyengat Island in 1847. Translated from the Malay

quotes.text: When the tongue is guarded, benefit will surely come of it.
quotes.source: Gurindam Dua Belas, third section, 1847. Translated from the Malay

quotes.text: Where you set your foot on the earth, there you hold up the sky.
quotes.source: Di mana bumi dipijak, di situ langit dijunjung. Follow the custom of the place you are in

quotes.text: Let the child die, but not the custom.
quotes.source: Biar mati anak, jangan mati adat. A hard saying about how much the old order was thought to matter

quotes.text: A just king is a king obeyed. A cruel king is a king defied.
quotes.source: Raja adil raja disembah, raja zalim raja disanggah. Linked in tradition with the story of Hang Jebat

quotes.text: If the ruler puts a single one of his subjects to shame, that shall be a sign that his kingdom will be destroyed by Almighty God.
quotes.by: The covenant of Sri Tri Buana and Demang Lebar Daun
quotes.source: Sejarah Melayu, the Malay Annals, compiled at the Johor court in 1612, after the translation of C. C. Brown

quotes.text: Never shall the Malays vanish from the earth.
quotes.source: Takkan Melayu hilang di dunia. A traditional saying given to the legendary admiral of Malacca

words.meaning: Custom; the right way of doing things
words.usage: The inherited code that governs ceremony, inheritance, dress and manners. It sits beside religious law, and people say that custom rests on it.
The quality most admired in a person. To do someone a kindness is to plant budi, and the debt can never be fully repaid.
Refined manners and gentle language together. The saying goes that language shows the people.
The ideal for speech, movement, weaving and feeling. Its opposite, kasar, is coarse.

words.meaning: Shame; modesty; a sense of propriety
words.usage: Knowing how to behave so as not to embarrass yourself or others. To make someone lose face is a grave offence.
A person’s or a people’s self-respect, to be guarded and never trampled.
Shown to elders, teachers and rulers by words, posture and precedence.
Decisions are talked through until everyone can accept them. A proverb says that agreement brings blessing.

words.meaning: Working together for the common good
words.usage: Neighbours join to build a house, clear a drain or cook for a wedding, with no payment but food and the certainty of help in return.
Houses on stilts among fruit trees, each household known to the others. English took the word compound from it.
Given for weddings, births, thanksgiving and the dead. The whole village is invited and the whole village cooks.

words.meaning: The sacred majesty of a ruler
words.usage: A mystical power believed to rest in the sultan. Subjects still greet him with the cry Daulat Tuanku.
The worst of crimes in the old order, believed to bring a curse on the offender.
The first virtue of a subject. Hang Tuah is its model, to a degree that later generations questioned.
Head of state and of religion in his state. Johor’s sultans trace their authority back to Malacca.
The highest office under the sultan. In 1699 a Bendahara took the throne of Johor.
The official in charge of police and the capital. The present royal house of Johor descends from the Temenggongs.
Commander of the fleet, a great office in a kingdom that lived by the sea.
The ruler’s residence and the centre of ceremony.
Boat-dwelling communities of the straits and islands, who served the sultans as pilots, rowers and fighters and were the kingdom’s strength at sea.
The general word for the vessels on which the Malay world traded, fished and went to war.

words.meaning: To leave home and seek one’s fortune
words.usage: Going abroad to trade, study or work, with the intention of returning with honour.
The first two lines give an image from nature or daily life. The second two give the meaning. They rhyme alternately and are exchanged in courtship, at feasts and in argument.
The first line sets a condition and the second its result. Raja Ali Haji’s twelve sets are the best known.
Romances and histories, read aloud from manuscripts to a listening circle.
The script of the old court, of letters between rulers and of every manuscript. Still used in Johor for religious and royal purposes.

words.meaning: The dagger with a wavy or straight blade
words.usage: A weapon, an heirloom and a mark of rank, forged with patterned steel and believed to have a character of its own.

words.meaning: Silk or cotton brocaded with gold thread
words.usage: The cloth of ceremony, worn by rulers and by every bride and groom.
Offered to a guest with lime, areca nut and gambier from a brass set. It opens every formal meeting and every marriage proposal.
Brought by traders from Hadhramaut and made Johor’s own, with quick neat footwork to lute and drums.

practices.name: Gentle speech
practices.instructions: Before you speak to anyone today, decide how you will speak. Greet each person first. Touch your hand lightly to your chest as you do it. Use their name or a term of respect. Keep your voice low and your words soft, especially when you disagree. The rule of this Onda is to speak softly.
practices.why: Budi bahasa, grace in manners and language, is the Malay ideal of speech. To be loud or blunt is to lack halus, refinement.
variations: Lower your voice a notch for the whole day.
Use a respectful title for an elder.
Say no gently, with a reason.

practices.name: A pantun a day
practices.instructions: Write one pantun. It has four lines of eight to twelve syllables, rhyming first with third and second with fourth. Lines one and two are the shadow: an image from what is in front of you, a tree, a boat, the weather, food. Lines three and four are the meaning: a thought or a wish. Read it aloud. It may be playful, loving or wise.
practices.why: The pantun is the best-loved Malay verse, shared at weddings, in courtship and in everyday talk. Its two halves, picture and meaning, are a form of wit.
variations: Answer a pantun with a pantun.

practices.name: The salam
practices.instructions: Greet each older person you meet today with the salam: take their hand lightly in both of yours, draw it to your own chest, and say good morning. Do not squeeze or shake. If you are not touching, bring your hand to your heart. It is a gesture of warmth and respect, hands first and then the heart.
practices.why: The Malay salam is a gentle, two-handed greeting that ends at the heart. It shows respect, particularly to elders.
variations: Greet your oldest relative this way.
Use it when you thank someone.

practices.name: Tea and kuih
practices.instructions: Make teh tarik, strong tea with condensed milk, pulled between two jugs until frothy, and eat it with a small kuih, a bite-sized sweet cake, such as kuih lapis or onde-onde. Sit at the table and share the tea with someone. The pulling cools the tea and makes it creamy. Enjoy the ritual.
practices.why: Teh tarik is the national drink of Malaysia, and morning tea with kuih is a cherished custom. It is a simple, sociable start to the day.
variations: Pull the tea three times between cups.
Share the kuih with a neighbour.
Try a new kuih each week.

practices.name: Make the house ready for a guest
practices.instructions: Sweep, wipe the table and put out a clean mat or cushion in your main room, in case someone calls today. Keep a jug of water and a plate of something small ready. Malay houses are kept open and ready for visitors, and a guest is received with the best you have. Make your space welcoming.
practices.why: A Malay house is always ready for visitors, and hospitality is a duty. Preparing for a guest, even an imaginary one, brings a welcome feeling.
variations: Put out a vase of flowers.

practices.name: One Malay word
practices.instructions: Learn one Malay word today and use it three times: terima kasih, thank you; selamat pagi, good morning; maaf, sorry; sama-sama, you are welcome; tolong, please help. Malay is spoken by more than 280 million people across Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei and Singapore. Try it on someone.
practices.why: Malay is a friendly, regular language, easy to start. A single word a day builds confidence quickly.
variations: Learn how to say your name.
Say thank you in Malay to a Malay speaker.

practices.name: Work with your neighbours
practices.instructions: Give half an hour to a job that belongs to everyone or to someone else on your street. Sweep a shared stair, clear a drain, tidy a common garden, carry for an older neighbour, cook for a family with a new baby or a death. Do it alongside others if you can, and do not make a fuss. The rule of this Onda is to do your share of the common work.
practices.why: Gotong-royong, communal work, is the Malay tradition of neighbours lifting a house, clearing a road or preparing a feast together. It is the root of community.
variations: Ask a neighbour if they need help.
Cook a dish for a shared meal.

practices.name: A game of congkak
practices.instructions: Play congkak, the Malay sowing game, with a friend. The board has two rows of small holes and a large store at each end. Players pick up seeds and sow them one by one round the board, capturing as they go. Use a congkak board, or two egg boxes and a handful of beads. Play a few rounds.
practices.why: Congkak has been played in the Malay world for centuries. It is a quick game of counting and planning, loved by children and adults.
variations: Make a board from egg cartons.

practices.name: Keep the ball up
practices.instructions: Play sepak raga with friends: stand in a circle and keep a light ball up with your feet, knees, shoulders and head, but not your hands. Count the passes. Use a rattan ball, a hacky sack or a light beach ball. Sepak raga has been played in the Malay world since at least the 15th century. Go gently and laugh at the misses.
practices.why: Sepak raga is an old Malay ball game that survives as the sport sepak takraw. The circle version is friendly and acrobatic.
variations: Count to fifty as a group.
Play in bare feet on grass.
Add a net for a game.

practices.name: Five stones
practices.instructions: Play batu seremban, a children’s game with five small stones. Throw the stones, pick one and toss it up, then gather the others before catching it. Then do it with two at a time, and so on. Use pebbles or beanbags. It is a game of hand skill passed from one generation to the next. Play with a child or a friend.
practices.why: Batu seremban is a village game played by girls and boys across the Malay world. It trains the hand and eye.
variations: Time yourself on the full round.

practices.name: Spin a top
practices.instructions: Spin a top, gasing, as Malay villagers did in contests after harvest. Use a wooden top with a string, or a modern one. Wind the string and throw it so that it spins on the ground. See whose lasts longest. Spinning contests used tops weighing several kilos, with their spin measured in minutes. Play outdoors on a flat surface.
practices.why: Gasing, top spinning, is a Malay pastime that grew into serious competition. A small top is easy to find and fun.

practices.name: Weave a paper mat
practices.instructions: Weave a small mat from strips of paper, the way mats of pandan leaf are woven in Malay villages. Cut strips of equal width in two colours. Lay half side by side and weave the others over and under. Glue the edges. Pandan weaving is a craft passed from mother to daughter, used for mats, baskets and bags.
practices.why: Anyaman, weaving with pandan, rattan or bamboo, is a Malay craft of long standing. A paper version teaches the over-under pattern.

practices.name: Eat together, with the right hand
practices.instructions: Share the evening meal. Set rice in the middle with a few dishes around it, and sit together, on a mat on the floor if you can. Wash your hands. Let the eldest begin. Take a little of each dish on to your rice and eat with your right hand, if you are comfortable doing so; otherwise use a spoon in your right hand. Pass dishes with the right hand and take only what you will finish. Honour your elders.
practices.why: Malay meals are shared from common dishes, with rice at the centre. Eating together, elders first, is a basic courtesy.

practices.name: One couplet of the Gurindam
practices.instructions: Read one couplet of Raja Ali Haji’s Twelve Gurindam, in Malay if you can and in translation if not. Read it twice, aloud. Then hold the day up to it. The third section alone will last a week: it speaks of guarding the eyes, ears, tongue and heart. Pick the couplet you most need, and sleep on it.
practices.why: The Gurindam Dua Belas, written in 1847 on Penyengat Island, is a famous book of twelve chapters of moral advice in rhyming couplets. Each line is a short lesson.
variations: Copy the couplet in a notebook.

practices.name: Berbalas pantun
practices.instructions: Hold a pantun exchange with a friend, berbalas pantun. One person recites a pantun, and the other must reply with one that answers it in meaning and rhyme. Take turns and be playful. At weddings and festivals this can last hours. Start with a pantun of greeting and end with one of farewell. Let it get cheeky and keep it kind.
practices.why: Berbalas pantun is a lively Malay tradition of verse repartee. It trains quick wit and affection.
variations: Do it with a child, simple rhymes.

practices.name: Listen to zapin
practices.instructions: Play zapin, the Malay dance music of Johor, with its gambus lute, drums and fast rhythms. Or play Ghazal Johor, with its violin and harmonium. Sit still and listen, or tap along. Zapin came with Arab traders and became a Malay art. It is lively and warm.
practices.why: Zapin and ghazal are the music of Johor’s court and villages. They show the meeting of Arab, Malay and Indian influences.
variations: Look at a picture of the gambus.

practices.name: A tale of Hang Tuah
practices.instructions: Tell or read a story of Hang Tuah, the legendary Malay admiral and friend of the Sultan of Melaka. Choose a short one, such as the duel with his friend Hang Jebat or his trip to China. Tell it with gestures. Ask the listeners what they would have done. Loyalty and friendship clash in these tales.
practices.why: The Hikayat Hang Tuah is the great Malay epic. Its stories of loyalty and betrayal have been retold for centuries.
variations: Watch an old film of it.

practices.name: Tea on the veranda
practices.instructions: Sit on a veranda, step or balcony with a glass of tea and watch the evening come. Greet passers-by and chat with neighbours. In a Malay kampung the front porch is the living room of the street. Sit without a screen and see who comes by. Offer tea.
practices.why: The veranda, serambi, is where Malay social life happens. Sitting out in the evening builds neighbourliness.
variations: Bring out a plate of fruit.

practices.name: A kenduri for neighbours
practices.instructions: Hold a small kenduri, a communal feast, for neighbours. Cook a big pot of rice and a couple of dishes, or ask everyone to bring one. Spread mats, wash hands and begin with a thank-you. Serve the elders first and eat together. Send a packet home with every guest. A kenduri marks births, weddings and good news, and the work is shared.
practices.why: The kenduri is the Malay feast, a shared meal that marks every important event. Preparing it together is gotong-royong at its best.
variations: Ask each household for a dish.

practices.name: A kampung games afternoon
practices.instructions: Hold an afternoon of kampung games in a yard or park: congkak, batu seremban, sepak raga, gasing, and a tug of war. Invite children and grown-ups. Give out small prizes to everyone. Serve iced drinks and fried snacks. These were the games of Malay village festivals. Keep it friendly and noisy.
practices.why: Traditional games are part of Malay festivals and school days. An afternoon of them is a joy for all ages.
variations: Invite elders to teach the games.

immersePlan.name: Read from the Malay Annals
immersePlan.text: Read a passage of the Sejarah Melayu, the court chronicle of the Melaka sultanate, such as the founding by Sang Nila Utama. Retell it.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Epic of Hang Tuah
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of the Malay epic of the hero admiral. Note the clash of loyalty and friendship.

immersePlan.name: Read from The Precious Gift
immersePlan.text: Read from Raja Ali Haji’s guide to kingship and conduct. Note one piece of advice.

immersePlan.name: Watch Puteri Gunung Ledang
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2004 film about the legendary princess of Mount Ledang and the Sultan of Melaka. It is colourful and lyrical.

immersePlan.name: Watch Bujang Lapok
immersePlan.text: Watch P. Ramlee’s 1957 comedy about three bachelors in a kampung. It is a classic and still funny.

immersePlan.name: Watch part of Hang Tuah
immersePlan.text: Watch an old film of the legendary admiral, 1956. Notice the costumes and the sword fights.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Ghazal Johor
immersePlan.text: Play the Malay court music of Johor with violin, gambus and harmonium. Listen for the sweet melodies.

immersePlan.name: Listen to zapin music
immersePlan.text: Play zapin with its lively gambus lute and hand drums, the dance music of Johor. Tap along and let your shoulders move.

immersePlan.name: Listen to P. Ramlee
immersePlan.text: Play songs by Malaysia’s favourite singer, composer and film star. Sing along to Getaran Jiwa.

immersePlan.name: Look at a keris
immersePlan.text: Look at the wavy-bladed Malay dagger, a symbol of status and spirit. Notice the pattern in the blade and the carved hilt.

immersePlan.name: Look at songket
immersePlan.text: Look at the gold-threaded cloth woven for royalty and weddings. Notice the pattern of rice grain and flowers.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Sultan Abu Bakar Mosque
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the white mosque in Johor Bahru, built in 1900 in Moorish and Malay style on a hill over the strait.

immersePlan.name: Cook or eat laksa Johor
immersePlan.text: Eat spaghetti-style noodles in a thick fish and coconut gravy, with lemongrass and sambal. Eat with a spoon and fork.

immersePlan.name: Make nasi lemak
immersePlan.text: Cook rice in coconut milk with pandan, and serve with sambal, fried anchovies, peanuts, cucumber and egg.

immersePlan.name: Taste otak-otak
immersePlan.text: Taste spiced fish paste grilled in a banana leaf parcel. Peel it open and enjoy the smoky scent.

immersePlan.name: Pull a teh tarik
immersePlan.text: Make strong tea with condensed milk and pull it between two jugs until frothy.

immersePlan.name: Make air bandung
immersePlan.text: Stir rose syrup into cold milk with ice. Serve in a tall glass.

immersePlan.name: Drink young coconut water
immersePlan.text: Drink from a young coconut straight from the shell, or from a carton. Scrape the soft flesh.

immersePlan.name: Learn about the sirih set
immersePlan.text: Read about the betel set that was offered to guests of honour at weddings and meetings. Offer a guest a small plate of fruit instead.

immersePlan.name: Greet with the salam
immersePlan.text: Greet an elder with the Malay salam, hands lightly touching and then brought to the heart.

immersePlan.name: Take your shoes off and use the right hand
immersePlan.text: Leave your shoes at the door and hand over and receive things with the right hand today.

immersePlan.name: Play congkak
immersePlan.text: Play the Malay sowing game with a friend, on a board or with egg boxes and beads.

immersePlan.name: Play sepak raga
immersePlan.text: Keep a light ball in the air with feet, knees and head. Count your passes.

immersePlan.name: Spin a gasing
immersePlan.text: Spin a top with a string and see how long it lasts. Challenge a friend.

immersePlan.name: Mark Hari Raya
immersePlan.text: Hari Raya Aidilfitri is the feast at the end of Ramadan, with visits, new clothes and open houses. Send a greeting, selamat Hari Raya, to a Muslim friend.

immersePlan.name: Look up Chingay in Johor Bahru
immersePlan.text: Look at the colourful street parade of the Chinese community in Johor Bahru, with lion dances and floats. Notice the mix of cultures.

immersePlan.name: Look up Kota Johor Lama
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the ruined old capital of Johor on the river at Kota Tinggi. Imagine the trading town.

immersePlan.name: Practise gotong-royong
immersePlan.text: Gotong-royong is working together for the common good. Do one shared job with a neighbour.

immersePlan.name: Practise budi bahasa
immersePlan.text: Budi bahasa is gracious manners. Speak softly and respectfully to everyone today.

immersePlan.name: Practise muafakat
immersePlan.text: Muafakat is agreement reached by consultation. Settle one decision by asking everyone involved what they think.

rules.why: Gentle words, low voice, no public shaming. Language shows the person.
A debt of budi is for life. Name it, honour it and pass it on.
Greet them first, give them precedence and listen before you speak.
Talk a matter through until all can accept it. Do not force a result.

rules.text: Do your share of the common work
rules.why: When neighbours labour, be there. When they feast or mourn, be there too.

rules.text: Follow the custom of the land
rules.why: Wherever you stand, respect the ways of the people whose ground it is.

read.title: Sejarah Melayu, the Malay Annals
read.creator: Compiled by Tun Sri Lanang; trans. C. C. Brown, or John Leyden
read.why: The founding work of Malay literature, put in order at the Johor court by its chief minister. It tells the rise and fall of Malacca in linked stories, witty and unsparing about rulers.

read.title: The Epic of Hang Tuah
read.creator: Anonymous, trans. Muhammad Haji Salleh
read.why: The adventures of the perfect Malay warrior and servant, written in Johor. Its central episode, in which Tuah kills his rebel friend for the sultan, has been argued over ever since.

read.title: The Precious Gift
read.creator: Raja Ali Haji, trans. Virginia Matheson and Barbara Watson Andaya
read.why: The Tuhfat al-Nafis, a history of Johor-Riau and the Bugis by the scholar of Penyengat. The first Malay history to give dates and weigh its sources.

read.title: The Hikayat Abdullah
read.creator: Munshi Abdullah, trans. A. H. Hill
read.why: The autobiography of a Malay teacher in Malacca and Singapore who knew Raffles and watched the old world give way. Sharp, modern and critical of rulers.

read.title: The Kingdom of Johor, 1641 to 1728
read.creator: Leonard Y. Andaya
read.why: The classic study of the sultanate at its height and through the crisis of the regicide.

read.title: Prince of Pirates
read.creator: Carl A. Trocki
read.why: How the Temenggongs turned from lords of the sea people into rulers of a modern state built on gambier and pepper.

watch.title: Hang Tuah
watch.creator: Phani Majumdar, with P. Ramlee
watch.why: The Shaw Brothers’ film of the legend, made in Singapore, with songs by its star. It ends with Tuah asking himself who was right.

watch.title: Hang Jebat
watch.creator: Hussain Haniff
watch.why: The same story from the rebel’s side. A dark, tightly made film that takes justice over loyalty.

watch.title: Puteri Gunung Ledang
watch.creator: Saw Teong Hin
watch.why: The sultan of Malacca sends Hang Tuah to win a mountain princess, who sets seven impossible conditions. Lavish, and the legend belongs to Johor’s own Mount Ledang.

watch.title: Bujang Lapok
watch.creator: P. Ramlee
watch.why: Three bachelors share lodgings in a Singapore kampung. The warmest picture of ordinary Malay neighbourhood life on film.

listen.title: Ghazal Johor
listen.creator: Groups such as Sri Maharani Ghazal of Muar
listen.why: Sung Malay poetry over harmonium, gambus lute, violin, guitar and tabla. It came from India by way of the Riau court and was shaped in the houses of Johor’s nobility.

listen.title: Zapin music
listen.creator: Zapin ensembles of Johor
listen.why: Gambus, small hand drums and violin driving the dance. Lancang Kuning and Ya Salam are standards.

listen.title: Songs of P. Ramlee
listen.creator: P. Ramlee
listen.why: The best loved Malay singer and composer. Getaran Jiwa is the one to begin with.

listen.title: Dondang Sayang
listen.creator: Singers of Malacca
listen.why: Two singers trade pantun over violin and drums, each trying to outdo the other in wit.

art.title: The keris
art.creator: Malay and Javanese smiths
art.why: A blade forged from layers of iron and nickel steel so that pale patterns appear in the metal, with a carved hilt and sheath. The state regalia of Johor include several.

art.title: Songket
art.creator: Weavers of the Malay Peninsula and Riau
art.why: Gold or silver thread is floated across a silk ground in bands of small repeated motifs: bamboo shoots, stars, cloves. Malaysia’s songket is on the UNESCO heritage list.

art.title: The Raffles manuscript of the Malay Annals
art.creator: Malay scribes
art.why: The oldest and best text of the Sejarah Melayu, in Jawi script, now in the Royal Asiatic Society, London.

art.title: The Sultan Abu Bakar State Mosque
art.creator: Johor Bahru
art.why: A white mosque on a hill above the strait whose four minarets look like English clock towers: the mark of a ruler who was at home in both worlds.

eat.title: Laksa Johor
eat.creator: Thick noodles in a rich fish and coconut gravy, with fresh herbs
eat.why: Made with spaghetti, a taste said to go back to Sultan Abu Bakar’s travels in Europe. Traditionally eaten with the hand.

eat.title: Nasi lemak
eat.creator: Rice cooked in coconut milk, with sambal, anchovies, peanuts and egg
eat.why: The breakfast of the peninsula, once wrapped in a banana leaf for the fields.

eat.title: Telur pindang
eat.creator: Eggs simmered for days with herbs and leaves until brown through
eat.why: A Johor speciality given to guests at weddings.

eat.title: Otak-otak
eat.creator: Spiced fish paste grilled in a palm leaf
eat.why: The snack of Muar, Johor’s old royal town on the river.

drink.title: Teh tarik
drink.creator: Strong tea with condensed milk, pulled between two cups until it froths
drink.why: The drink of every roadside stall, poured from a height.

drink.title: Air bandung
drink.creator: Rose syrup with milk, over ice
drink.why: Pink and sweet, served at weddings and at the breaking of the fast.

drink.title: Young coconut water
drink.creator: Drunk from the shell
drink.why: The plainest refreshment of the coast.

customs.title: Offering sirih
customs.creator: The betel set
customs.why: A brass or silver box with leaf, lime, nut and gambier is set before guests. It begins formal talks, and a marriage proposal is made by presenting one.

customs.title: The salam
customs.creator: Hands, then the heart
customs.why: Take the other person’s hand lightly in both of yours, then bring your hand to your chest. The young kiss the hand of an elder.

customs.title: Shoes off, right hand only
customs.creator: At the door and at the mat
customs.why: Outdoor shoes stay on the steps. Food and gifts are given and taken with the right hand.

customs.title: King and queen for a day
customs.creator: The wedding dais
customs.why: Bride and groom sit in state in songket on a decorated dais and are blessed with scented water and rice, treated for that day as royalty.

games.title: Congkak
games.creator: Board game · Malay world
games.why: A boat-shaped board with two rows of seven holes and a store at each end. Players sow shells or seeds round it. Once a game of palace women, now of everyone.

games.title: Sepak raga
games.creator: Ball game · Malay world
games.why: A woven rattan ball kept in the air with feet, knees and head. The Malay Annals record a death over a game. Its modern form over a net is sepak takraw.

games.title: Gasing
games.creator: Top spinning · Malay Peninsula
games.why: Heavy wooden tops launched with a rope. Contests are for the longest spin or for knocking a rival’s top out of the ring.

games.title: Batu seremban
games.creator: Five stones · Malay world
games.why: Five small stones or beanbags tossed and caught in a set order of rising difficulty. Played by children on any floor.

festivals.title: Hari Raya Aidilfitri
festivals.creator: At the end of Ramadan, by the lunar calendar
festivals.why: Families ask one another’s forgiveness, visit graves and keep open house, with everyone of every faith welcome to come in and eat.

festivals.title: The Sultan of Johor’s birthday
festivals.creator: 23 March
festivals.why: A public holiday in the state, with an investiture at the palace and prayers at the state mosque.

festivals.title: Chingay in Johor Bahru
festivals.creator: The 21st day of the first lunar month, in February or March
festivals.why: The five Chinese clans of the city carry their deities through the streets together by night. A tradition of the gambier and pepper settlers that the sultans protected, more than a century old.

places.title: Kota Johor Lama
places.creator: Kota Tinggi, Johor, Malaysia
places.why: The earth ramparts of the sixteenth-century capital on a bend of the Johor River, with a small museum. Portuguese ships came up this river to burn it in 1587.

places.title: Kampung Makam
places.creator: Kota Tinggi, Johor, Malaysia
places.why: The tomb of Sultan Mahmud II, killed in 1699 while being carried on a litter, with whom the line of Malacca ended. The graves of ministers and of the admiral who struck him are near by.

places.title: The Sultan Abu Bakar State Mosque and the Grand Palace
places.creator: Johor Bahru, Johor, Malaysia
places.why: The mosque is open outside prayer times to visitors who dress modestly. The palace of 1866 stands in gardens beside the strait. Check whether its museum is open.

places.title: Penyengat Island
places.creator: Off Tanjung Pinang, Riau Islands, Indonesia
places.why: The small island seat of the Bugis viceroys. A yellow mosque said to have egg white in its mortar, royal tombs and the grave of Raja Ali Haji. Ten minutes by boat.

places.title: Kampong Glam
places.creator: Singapore
places.why: The palace of Sultan Hussein, now the Malay Heritage Centre, and the Sultan Mosque beside it, in the quarter set aside for the Johor royal house in 1819.

places.title: Muar
places.creator: Johor, Malaysia
places.why: Bandar Maharani, the royal town on the river, with fine colonial offices, a customs house and some of the best food in the state.

ethics.title: Budi
ethics.text: Kindness given freely and remembered for life. A person without budi is no one, whatever their wealth.
ethics.practice: Do a kindness today that cannot be returned.

ethics.title: Courtesy
ethics.text: Gentle speech and correct conduct protect everyone’s dignity.
ethics.practice: Soften one thing you were going to say sharply.

ethics.title: Loyalty
ethics.text: Stand by those to whom you owe allegiance: ruler, teacher, friend, family.
ethics.practice: Be reliable today to someone who is counting on you.

ethics.title: Shame and modesty
ethics.text: A proper sense of malu keeps a person from boasting, grabbing and exposing others.
ethics.practice: Let someone else take the credit.

ethics.title: Consensus
ethics.text: A decision everyone can live with is better than a quick one that divides.
ethics.practice: In one disagreement today, look for the answer that both sides can accept.

ethics.title: Justice in rulers
ethics.text: The covenant runs both ways. The people owe loyalty, and the ruler owes them freedom from humiliation.
ethics.practice: If you have power over someone, check that you have not shamed them.

philosophy.title: The debt of kindness
philosophy.text: Money debts can be cleared. What you owe to those who were good to you cannot, and that is what ties a community together.
philosophy.practice: List three people whose kindness made you. Have you told them?

philosophy.title: Language shows the people
philosophy.text: How a person speaks reveals their upbringing and their heart. Refinement of words is refinement of self.
philosophy.practice: Listen to yourself for an hour. What does your speech say about you?

philosophy.title: The covenant
philosophy.text: In the Malay Annals the first ruler and the first chief swear an oath: subjects will never rebel, and rulers will never shame their subjects. A kingdom falls when either side breaks it.
philosophy.practice: What unwritten covenant holds between you and those you lead or follow?

philosophy.title: Tuah and Jebat
philosophy.text: Hang Tuah kills his friend out of loyalty to an unjust king. Hang Jebat rebels for the sake of his friend. Malays have debated for three centuries which was the hero.
philosophy.practice: When loyalty and justice part, which do you follow?

philosophy.title: Custom and the sky
philosophy.text: Wherever you stand, the local order is the sky above you. A guest adapts.
philosophy.practice: Where are you a guest, and are you behaving like one?

philosophy.title: Shadow and meaning
philosophy.text: A pantun says the important thing sideways, through an image. Truth told indirectly can be heard.
philosophy.practice: What do you need to say that would be better said through a picture?

philosophy.title: A kingdom of water
philosophy.text: Johor was a network of rivers, straits and loyal seafarers. Its capitals moved many times. The kingdom was its people and its trade, wherever the court sat.
philosophy.practice: What in your life would survive if its buildings were lost?

philosophy.title: Many peoples, one roof
philosophy.text: Malays, Bugis, sea people, Chinese planters, Arabs and Indians all had a place under the sultans. The state’s skill was in giving each a role.
philosophy.practice: Who around you has no acknowledged place?

journal: Whose kindness are you carrying, and how will you honour it?
How did you speak today?
Whom did you shame, even slightly?
What custom did you follow that is not your own?
What did you do alongside your neighbours?
Who ate with you?
What pantun did the day suggest?
Which elder did you greet first?
Where did you raise your voice?
What did you refuse, and how gently?
What decision did you force that should have been agreed?
To whom are you loyal, and are they worthy of it?
Where did loyalty and justice pull apart?
What did you guard today: eyes, ears, tongue, hands, stomach or feet?
What did you let slip?
Whose face did you save?
Who taught you your manners?
What do you owe your teacher?
What have you gone abroad to seek?
What will you bring home?
Whom did you welcome at the door?
What did you give with your right hand?
What common work have you been avoiding?
Who near you is celebrating or grieving, and were you there?
What would the covenant say about how you use your authority?
What did you say sideways that was understood?
What part of your heritage is in danger of vanishing?
Where is your kampung?
What kindness did you plant today?
What debt will you carry to the grave, gladly?
reflect: Which debts of kindness did you name?
What did working with neighbours build?
Where do you stand between Tuah and Jebat?

intro: In the fifteenth century the port of Malacca, on the strait that bears its name, was the richest trading city in Southeast Asia and the centre of the Malay world. Its rulers had adopted Islam, its language had become the common tongue of trade from Sumatra to the Spice Islands, and its court set the pattern of Malay custom, dress and ceremony. In 1511 a Portuguese fleet took it by storm.

The sultan escaped. After years of wandering, his son Alauddin Riayat Shah established a new capital on the Johor River in about 1528. The Sultanate of Johor regarded itself as Malacca continued: it had the old royal line, the regalia and the loyalty of the Orang Laut, the sea people whose boats controlled the straits. For a century it fought a three-cornered war with the Portuguese and with the Sumatran kingdom of Aceh. Its capital was burned and moved many times. In 1641 it helped the Dutch take Malacca and entered its most prosperous age, as a free port for Chinese, Indian, Arab and European traders.

It was at the Johor court in 1612 that the chief minister, Tun Sri Lanang, was commanded to set down the Sejarah Melayu, the Malay Annals, so that later generations would know the customs and the history of the Malay kings. The book is the foundation of Malay literature. At its heart is a covenant: subjects will never rebel, and rulers will never put a subject to shame.

In 1699 that covenant was tested. The young sultan, a cruel and unstable man, was stabbed to death by one of his nobles while being carried to the mosque. He left no heir, and the line of Malacca ended. The chief minister took the throne, a Sumatran pretender challenged him, and Bugis warriors from Sulawesi were called in. From 1722 the kingdom, now centred on the Riau islands, was run by Bugis viceroys under Malay sultans. Their island of Penyengat became the great centre of Malay learning, where Raja Ali Haji wrote history, grammar and the Twelve Gurindam.

In 1819 Stamford Raffles obtained Singapore from the Temenggong, the minister who governed the southern part of the kingdom, and from a prince he recognised as sultan for the purpose. Five years later Britain and the Netherlands drew a line through the straits that cut the old kingdom in two. The mainland half was rebuilt by the Temenggong’s family. Daeng Ibrahim opened the jungle to Chinese pepper and gambier planters. His son Abu Bakar founded Johor Bahru, travelled to Europe, became a friend of Queen Victoria, took the title of sultan and in 1895 gave his state a written constitution, the first in the Malay states.
Johor joined the Federation of Malaya in 1948 and independent Malaya in 1957. Its sultans still reign, and take their turn as king of Malaysia.

This Onda takes its practices from the culture that the court preserved and the villages lived: gentle speech, the daily pantun, shared labour, the shared meal and a couplet of the Gurindam at night. It is the culture of living people in Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and you are a guest in it.
guide.origin: The southern Malay Peninsula, the Johor River, and the islands of Riau and Singapore
guide.era: Founded in 1528 by the heir of Malacca. The royal house of Johor reigns today as one of Malaysia’s nine

figures.name: Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah II
figures.bio: Son of the last sultan of Malacca and founder of Johor. He died a captive in Aceh.

figures.name: Hang Tuah
figures.bio: The admiral of Malacca, hero of the epic written in Johor. Whether he lived is uncertain. What he stands for is not.

figures.name: Tun Sri Lanang
figures.bio: Chief minister of Johor and compiler of the Malay Annals. Carried off to Aceh in 1613, he ended his life as a ruler there.

figures.name: Laksamana Tun Abdul Jamil
figures.bio: The admiral who rebuilt Johor’s trade and power after a Sumatran rival sacked its capital in 1673.

figures.name: Sultan Mahmud II
figures.bio: The last of the Malacca line, remembered as the king who died on the litter. His murder haunted Malay political thought.

figures.name: Daeng Marewah
figures.bio: The first Bugis viceroy, installed in 1722. He and his four brothers changed the balance of the Malay world.

figures.name: Raja Haji Fisabilillah
figures.bio: The fourth Bugis viceroy, who died attacking the Dutch at Malacca. A national hero of Indonesia.

figures.name: Raja Ali Haji
figures.bio: His grandson: historian, poet, grammarian and jurist of Penyengat, and the author of the first Malay dictionary by a Malay.

figures.name: Sultan Hussein Shah
figures.bio: The elder prince passed over for the throne, whom Raffles recognised as sultan in 1819 in order to obtain Singapore.

figures.name: Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim
figures.bio: He turned from suppressing piracy to granting river concessions to Chinese planters, and made Johor rich.

figures.name: Sultan Abu Bakar
figures.bio: The father of modern Johor. English-educated, a shrewd diplomat and builder, he kept his state independent of British control in his lifetime.

figures.name: Onn Jaafar
figures.bio: Chief minister of Johor and founder of the United Malays National Organisation in 1946, at the Grand Palace in Johor Bahru.

history.detail: A prince from Palembang founds a port on the strait. Within a century it is the meeting point of the Indian Ocean and China trades.
Afonso de Albuquerque takes the city. Sultan Mahmud Shah retreats south and dies in Sumatra in 1528.
His son sets up a capital on the upper Johor River. It will move more than twenty times in the next two centuries.
A Portuguese fleet sails up the river and destroys the fortified capital.

history.what: The Malay Annals; the Acehnese raid
history.detail: Tun Sri Lanang begins the chronicle. The following year Aceh sacks the capital and carries off the court.
Johor fights as their ally and is rewarded with trading privileges and half a century of prosperity.
Sultan Mahmud II is killed at Kota Tinggi. The chief minister ascends the throne as the first of a new dynasty.
A prince from Sumatra claiming to be the dead sultan’s son seizes Johor. Five Bugis brothers expel him and take the office of viceroy.
After the death of Raja Haji the Dutch garrison the capital. The kingdom never fully recovers its independence.
Raffles signs a treaty with the Temenggong and with Hussein, whom he installs as sultan, for a British trading post.
The Anglo-Dutch Treaty puts the peninsula and Singapore under Britain and the Riau and Lingga islands under the Netherlands.
The sultan’s heir cedes the state to the Temenggong. A new capital is laid out on the strait and later named Johor Bahru.
Abu Bakar is recognised as sultan by Britain. Shortly before his death he proclaims a written constitution.
Johor accepts a British general adviser in 1914, joins the Federation of Malaya in 1948 and becomes part of an independent country in 1957.

concepts.detail: The ruler carries a sacred force, and to defy him is to invite a curse. The idea held Malay kingdoms together and made the killing of 1699 a catastrophe.
The mythical contract in the Malay Annals between the first king and the chief of the people, which binds rulers not to humiliate and subjects not to rebel.
The rules of ceremony, rank, marriage and inheritance, handed down and adjusted by agreement. The saying is that custom rests on religious law, and religious law on the Book.
A cluster of kindness, good sense and gratitude. Malay proverbs, pantun and tales return to it more than to any other idea.
Chief minister, minister of justice, admiral and treasurer. The pattern was inherited from Malacca, and two of the offices in turn founded dynasties in Johor.
Orang Laut groups owed service to the ruler personally, each with its own task. Their withdrawal after the regicide left the new dynasty exposed.
From 1722 a Bugis Yang Dipertuan Muda held real power beside a Malay sultan, sealed by an oath of loyalty and by marriages.
Chinese headmen were granted rights over a river valley to plant gambier and pepper, collect taxes and keep order. It opened the interior of Johor in a generation.
Decisions were reached in council by talking until agreement emerged. Johor’s state motto pairs it with trust in God.

facts.text: The capital of Johor moved at least twenty times between 1528 and 1855, usually along the Johor River.
The word Johor is thought to come from the Arabic jauhar, a jewel.
Johor is the only Malaysian state with its own military force, founded by Sultan Abu Bakar in 1886.
The Malay Annals survive in some thirty manuscripts, no two alike.
Singapore, the Riau Islands of Indonesia and the Malaysian state of Johor were all one kingdom until 1824.
The pantun form reached French poetry through a note in a book by Victor Hugo in 1829.

glossary.meaning: The fifteenth-century sultanate from which Johor claimed descent
The island half of the kingdom, under Dutch influence after 1824
A seafaring people of South Sulawesi who settled widely in the Malay world
The viceroy, literally the junior ruler
A plant extract used in tanning and with betel, Johor’s main export in the nineteenth century
The form of address to a ruler

sensitivity.note: The Johor Sultanate is a living monarchy and Malay culture is a living culture, shared across Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Brunei. This Onda borrows everyday courtesies and verse forms. It is written by outsiders and should be checked by Malay readers.
requiredCaveats: The sultan and the royal house are held in deep respect in Johor. Speak of them accordingly.
Malay custom is closely tied to Islam. The practices here are the social ones. They are not a substitute for the faith, and they do not require it.
The old order rested on rank, and on debt bondage and slavery, which the sea people and others bore. Loyalty was not always freely given.
Malays, Bugis, Orang Laut and the Chinese and Indian communities of Johor each have their own account of this history.
